newsitem.title: USA: NYC Council presents revenue forecasts, tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: NYC Council presents revenue forecasts, tax cuts.

text.p: The New York City Council on Wednesday presented its revenue forecasts and tax proposals for the current and next fiscal years.
The council projected $146 million more in tax revenues than previously estimated for the current fiscal year and $356 million more in tax revenues for fiscal year 1998, which begins July 1.
The council also proposed that the city create a "rainy day" fund with $225 million in projected tax revenues for fiscal 1998 and cut taxes by $168 million for the same period.
City Council Speaker Peter Vallone, in prepared remarks, criticized New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani for lacking "a vision for job growth."

The Council's proposed tax cuts, which would continue through fiscal 2001, when they total $353 million, would try to encourage the owners of partnerships and small businesses to live and work in New York City, instead of moving to a neighboring states or county.

The biggest share of the tax cuts proposed by the City Council would be for an unincorporated business tax credit on the personal income tax, a break that would add up to $76 million in fiscal 1998 and $185 million in 2001.
The Giuliani Administration has proposed eliminating the unincorporated business tax but not offered business owners an incentive to stay in the city, a Council spokeswoman said.

A $45 million program to boost employment in "emerging industries" -- defined as high-tech areas like software -- would give qualified companies a five-year tax moratorium if they agreed to keep at least 75 percent of their payroll in the city for the next 10 years and employed less than 100 workers during the initial period of the moratorium.

Noting that the expected rise in revenues, which exceeds the Giuliani Administration's forecasts, mostly will come from one industry -- Wall Street brokerage houses -- the City Council Speaker noted that this leaves New York City vulnerable to a market downturn.

Asked how the Council would close huge, out-year budget gaps, he told reporters at a news conference: "We are creating structural balance by diversification." Since 1990, Vallone said the city has closed budget gaps that totaled $14 billion.
